cards.front: Cerebellar damage does not paralyse. What does it do to movement, and what is the cerebellum's usual job?
cards.back: The person moves, but badly: reaches overshoot and the hand shakes near the target. The cerebellum does not usually start movements; it makes them accurate and keeps them accurate.
cards.quote: It does not usually start movements on its own. It makes them accurate

cards.front: In cerebellar motor control, a {{c1::prediction}} is a learned estimate of what a command will do, used before the senses report the result.
cards.quote: A prediction, here, is a learned estimate of what a command will do, used before the senses report the result.
cards.section: Moving badly, not weakly: three puzzles

cards.front: In motor learning, an {{c1::error}} is the mismatch between the predicted or intended result and the observed one.
cards.quote: An error is the mismatch between the predicted or intended result and the observed one.
cards.section: Moving badly, not weakly: three puzzles

cards.front: The cerebellar circuit can be drawn with three roles: context, error and output. Which element fills each role?
cards.back: Context: many parallel fibres. Error (the teaching signal, in the classical model): one climbing fibre. Output: steadily firing nuclear neurons, with Purkinje cells acting as the brake.
cards.quote: One line climbs up from below: it carries the error (the teaching signal, in the classical model).

cards.front: What do mossy fibres bring into the cerebellum, and from where?
cards.back: Through the pontine nuclei, signals from the cerebral cortex, including a copy of the commands it is sending; from the spinal cord and vestibular nuclei, signals about what the body senses.
cards.quote: Through the pontine nuclei come signals from the cerebral cortex, including a copy of the commands it is sending
cards.section: Context: mossy fibres, granule cells, parallel fibres

cards.front: Trace the context pathway in the cerebellar cortex from mossy fibre to Purkinje cell.
cards.back: Mossy fibres excite granule cells in the deepest layer. Each granule-cell axon rises to the molecular layer, splits, and runs as a parallel fibre through the dendrites of many Purkinje cells.
cards.quote: Each granule cell sends its axon up to the outer, molecular layer, where it splits and runs along the fold as a parallel fibre.
cards.section: Context: mossy fibres, granule cells, parallel fibres

cards.front: Where do cerebellar climbing fibres come from, and how many does an adult Purkinje cell receive?
cards.back: From the inferior olive in the medulla, crossing the midline. Each adult Purkinje cell receives one climbing fibre, which makes many contacts along its dendrite.
cards.quote: Each adult Purkinje cell receives one climbing fibre, which winds up its dendrite and makes many contacts along it.
cards.section: The teaching signal: one climbing fibre

cards.front: What transmitter do Purkinje cells release, and which neurons do they inhibit?
cards.back: GABA. They inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei; in the vestibulocerebellum some inhibit the vestibular nuclei directly. They are the only output cells of the cerebellar cortex.
cards.quote: Purkinje cells are the only output cells of the cerebellar cortex, and they release GABA.
cards.section: The output: a brake on nuclei that are already running

cards.front: If the cerebellar cortex only inhibits, where does cerebellar output come from?
cards.back: From the deep nuclei and, for some vestibulocerebellar pathways, the vestibular nuclei. Many nuclear neurons fire steadily, driven by pacemaking and by excitatory mossy- and climbing-fibre collaterals. Purkinje cells shape that firing by timed inhibition.
cards.why: A Purkinje cell is a foot on the brake of a car whose engine is already running.
cards.quote: So the nuclei carry the output, and the cortex sculpts it by timed inhibition.
cards.section: The output: a brake on nuclei that are already running

cards.front: State the classical Marr-Albus-Ito learning rule at the parallel-fibre to Purkinje-cell synapse, in both directions.
cards.back: A well-timed climbing-fibre error signal can weaken the parallel-fibre synapses active at the right moment. Parallel-fibre activity without a paired climbing-fibre signal can strengthen them.
cards.quote: Parallel-fibre activity without a paired climbing-fibre signal can strengthen the same synapses, so a correction can run either way.
cards.section: The output: a brake on nuclei that are already running

cards.front: In a Purkinje-cell recording, how do simple spikes and complex spikes differ in shape, rate and cause?
cards.back: Simple spikes: ordinary action potentials at tens per second, with firing set by intrinsic excitability and excitatory and inhibitory inputs; parallel-fibre input changes the rate. Complex spikes: a large spike plus wavelets, one per climbing-fibre event, about one per second.
cards.quote: Complex spikes are large spikes followed by smaller wavelets, one for each climbing-fibre event, at around one per second.

cards.front: A Purkinje cell is recorded for 5 s: 300 simple spikes and 6 complex spikes, each complex spike followed by a 30 ms pause. Find both rates and the percent of the record spent paused. Which signal carries most ongoing output?
cards.back: Rate = count / time. Simple: 300 / 5 s = 60 Hz. Complex: 6 / 5 s = 1.2 Hz. Paused: 6 × 30 ms = 180 ms of 5000 ms = 3.6%. Simple spikes carry most ongoing output.
cards.why: In the classical model the rare complex spikes mainly teach, marking when the climbing fibre fired.
cards.quote: Simple spikes: 130 / 2 s = 65 Hz. Complex spikes: 2 / 2 s = 1 Hz.

cards.front: In the rabbit cerebellum, parallel fibres were stimulated after three conditions: parallel fibres alone, climbing fibre alone, or both together. What was the result, and what did it show?
cards.back: Only pairing left the parallel-fibre response smaller, for at least an hour. This is cerebellar long-term depression (LTD): co-activity with the climbing fibre weakens the synapse.
cards.quote: Under these test conditions, only pairing produced a long-lasting depression of parallel-fibre to Purkinje transmission.

cards.front: After cerebellar LTD, the same context recurs with other inputs unchanged. Does the deep-nucleus output fire more or less, and why?
cards.back: More. Weaker parallel-fibre drive means less Purkinje firing, so less inhibition of a nucleus that is already firing: two negatives make a positive.
cards.quote: The foot presses the brake less, so the nucleus, already firing, speeds up: two negatives make a positive.

cards.front: A drug blocks the action of Purkinje-cell GABA on deep cerebellar nuclear neurons. Predict the nuclear firing rate and what happens to the cortex's control of output timing.
cards.back: Nuclear firing rises, because pacemaking and excitatory collaterals continue with no brake. The cortex can no longer shape output by timed inhibition, so its timing contribution is lost.
cards.why: Rests on: Purkinje cells release GABA onto nuclei that fire steadily on their own, and their inhibition slows or pauses that firing.
cards.quote: Purkinje inhibition slows or pauses that firing.
cards.section: The output: a brake on nuclei that are already running

cards.front: In mouse-slice experiments, floccular LTD was strongest for parallel fibres active about 120 ms before the climbing fibre. Why does that interval make sense?
cards.back: A visual error reaches the flocculus through climbing fibres roughly a tenth of a second late. Fibres active shortly before carry the context in which the mistake was made.
cards.quote: In the flocculus, which steers eye movements, LTD is strongest for parallel fibres active about 120 ms before the climbing fibre.
cards.section: The timing: correcting before the error

cards.front: What is anticipatory control, the sense in which the cerebellum is said to predict?
cards.back: When the same context recurs, the learned change acts before the delayed error arrives: a correction from a learned estimate rather than from waiting for feedback.
cards.quote: That is anticipatory control, a correction from a learned estimate rather than from waiting for feedback
cards.section: The timing: correcting before the error

cards.front: Suppose a cerebellar region received its climbing-fibre error with almost no delay after the mistake. Which parallel fibres should its timing rule favour for LTD, compared with the flocculus, and why?
cards.back: Fibres active much closer in time to the climbing fibre than the flocculus's roughly 120 ms. The rule should tag the context in which the mistake was made, and a shorter delay brings that context closer to the error.
cards.why: Rests on: depressed fibres carry the context of the mistake, and the best interval differs between cerebellar regions.
cards.quote: So the fibres active shortly before the climbing fibre carry the context in which the mistake was made, not the one in which it was noticed.
cards.section: The timing: correcting before the error

cards.front: A mouse's eyes reach 9 degrees/s in response to a 12 degrees/s head turn. What is its vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) gain, and what gain keeps a distant target still?
cards.back: Gain = eye-speed amplitude / head-speed amplitude = 9 / 12 = 0.75. A gain of 1 keeps the image of a distant target still.
cards.quote: Its gain is eye-speed amplitude divided by head-speed amplitude.
cards.section: A worked example: the vestibulo-ocular reflex

cards.front: Magnifying glasses are put on. In Ito's account of the horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex, how does the gain come to rise?
cards.back: The old gain moves the eyes too little, so the image slips. Slip drives floccular climbing fibres; parallel-fibre synapses carrying the head-turn signal shortly before the climbing-fibre signal can be depressed; Purkinje cells fire less in the ipsiversive phase, boosting compensatory drive.
cards.quote: That retinal slip is the error, and the gain must rise.
cards.section: A worked example: the vestibulo-ocular reflex

cards.front: Glasses that shrink the world make the eyes move too much during the vestibulo-ocular reflex. Which way must the gain change, and can LTD in a single brake channel produce it?
cards.back: The gain must fall. In one channel, LTD only releases the brake and raises output, so it cannot lower it; strengthening the same synapses would press the brake harder.
cards.why: The real reflex is phase-specific, so less Purkinje firing in the other phase could in principle lower the gain. Direction alone does not identify the mechanism.
cards.quote: In the one-channel brake cartoon, LTD only releases the brake, so it cannot lower that channel's output
cards.section: A worked example: the vestibulo-ocular reflex

cards.front: Floccular climbing fibres raise their rate above a baseline of about one per second for slip one way and lower it for slip the other way. Using the brake model, how could LTD alone, or LTD plus LTP, correct errors in both directions?
cards.back: In one channel, LTD only releases the brake and LTP reverses it. Across opposing channels or phases of a movement, releasing the brake in the opposite channel shifts net output the other way, so LTD alone could do it.
cards.quote: across opposing channels or phases of a movement, LTD alone could still shift behaviour either way

cards.front: In mice, climbing fibres were driven with light (optogenetics) during head rotation. Gain-increase VOR learning occurred; the tested pairing did not drive gain-decrease learning. What does this show about the teaching signal?
cards.back: The teacher can be gated: the same climbing-fibre signal taught one direction of learning and not the other.
cards.quote: The same signal taught in one direction of learning and not the other.

cards.front: Three mouse lines lacking parallel-fibre LTD in standard slice tests learned VOR adaptation, eyeblink conditioning and a stepping task normally. Give two explanations that keep the cerebellum as a site of learning.
cards.back: Learning may use plasticity at other sites, such as the deep nuclei. Or LTD was present but missed: modified protocols later induced LTD in slices from two of the lines.
cards.quote: Plasticity is thought to occur at several sites, including the deep nuclei, which may hold part of the long-term memory.

cards.front: Propose an experiment to ask whether a learned VOR gain change is stored in the flocculus or in the vestibular nuclei it controls.
cards.back: Train a gain increase, then inactivate the flocculus and re-measure the gain without visual feedback. Persistence of the adapted gain would be consistent with a downstream trace; loss would mean the flocculus is needed for storage or expression, without telling which.
cards.why: Rests on: plasticity is thought to occur at several sites, and the deep nuclei may hold part of the long-term memory.
cards.quote: Where the VOR memory is stored, in the flocculus or in the vestibular nuclei it controls, was argued for years.

cards.front: In Ito's account of horizontal VOR gain-increase training with magnifying glasses, what changes would you expect in a suitably tuned floccular Purkinje cell's complex spikes and ipsiversive-phase simple spikes?
cards.back: Retinal slip can recruit the climbing-fibre teaching signal, so complex spikes may rise (a hypothesis, not a guaranteed trajectory). The learned change lowers ipsiversive-phase simple-spike firing, reducing inhibition of vestibular targets. A lasting simple-spike drop was seen in some monkey cells in a separate changed-load task.
cards.why: Rests on: retinal slip drives climbing fibres, pairing depresses parallel fibres, and in some adapting monkey cells complex spikes rose and simple-spike responses stayed lower.
cards.quote: While the monkeys adapted, complex spikes became more frequent.
cards.section: What a learning Purkinje cell looks like

cards.front: Besides movement errors, what did climbing fibres signal in mice trained on a rewarded task?
cards.back: Reward expectation, delivery and omission.
cards.quote: In mice trained on a rewarded task they also signalled reward expectation, delivery and omission

cards.front: After prism adaptation, throws miss the opposite way once the goggles come off. What does this after-effect show, and is the change purely motor?
cards.back: The mapping between seeing and moving was recalibrated and outlasts the goggles. It is not purely motor: part can be sensory, shifts in where you see and feel your arm.
cards.quote: Part of the change is sensory: it can include shifts in where you see and feel your arm, not only in the motor command.

cards.front: Prisms make a first throw land 30 cm right of target. Each throw corrects a fixed fraction k = 0.40 of the remaining error, nothing else changing. Find the error after 3 corrections and how many corrections bring it below 3 cm.
cards.back: Error = E0 × (1 − k)^n. After 3: 30 × 0.6^3 = 6.48 cm. Below 3 cm needs 0.6^n < 0.1: n > ln 0.1 / ln 0.6 = 4.51, so 5 corrections, leaving 2.33 cm.
cards.quote: error after n corrections = E0 × (1 − k)^n

cards.front: In the fixed-fraction prism model, a thrower starts 30 cm right of target and after 5 corrections has 2.33 cm of error left. The prisms are removed. Where does the next throw land, and why are real after-effects usually smaller?
cards.back: Learned correction = 30 − 2.33 = 27.67 cm leftward, so the throw lands about 27.7 cm left. Real after-effects are smaller partly because people drop a deliberate aiming strategy once the prisms are off.
cards.quote: In real throwers the after-effect is usually smaller than the full correction, partly because part of the correction is a deliberate aiming strategy

cards.front: Two people adapt to the same prisms for the same number of throws. One has olivocerebellar damage and corrects a smaller fraction of the error per throw. Compare their final error and after-effect.
cards.back: The slow learner ends with a larger remaining error and a smaller after-effect: little was learned, so little is left to apply once the prisms come off.
cards.why: The model cannot say which part of the pathway is damaged.
cards.quote: after the same number of throws, slow learning leaves both a large error and a small after-effect

cards.front: On a split-belt treadmill, one leg is driven faster than the other. Compared with controls, what do people with cerebellar damage keep and what do they lose?
cards.back: They keep the quick, reactive adjustments within each step but show disrupted predictive adaptation, the kind that leaves an after-effect when the belts are equalized.
cards.quote: In this task, the cerebellum seemed needed for predicting more than for reacting.

cards.front: A person with cerebellar damage walks on a split-belt treadmill for several minutes, then the belts are equalized. Predict the after-effect compared with a control, and link it to what the prism after-effect measures.
cards.back: Little after-effect. In both tasks the after-effect reads out a learned predictive change. Reactive within-step corrections leave none, and those are what the patient keeps.
cards.why: Rests on: after-effects mark recalibration that outlasts the perturbation; cerebellar damage spares reactive and disrupts predictive adaptation.
cards.quote: showed disrupted predictive adaptation, the kind that leaves an after-effect when the belts are equalized

cards.front: Design an experiment to tell whether cerebellum-dependent adaptation learns from sensory prediction error or from having made a corrective movement.
cards.back: Rotate the cursor showing the hand. Shooting: fast reaches with no online correction. Pointing: correction allowed. Match visual errors; measure after-effects with rotation removed and feedback withheld. If correction teaches, shooting adapts less; if prediction error teaches, both adapt.
cards.why: When run, controls adapted in both conditions and people with hereditary cerebellar ataxia adapted less in both, supporting prediction error.
cards.quote: If making a correction is what teaches, shooting should adapt less. If prediction error teaches, both should adapt.

cards.front: On one account, why does losing the cerebellum's prediction cause overshoot and a tremor that grows near the target?
cards.back: On this account, movement leans more on sensory feedback, and visual feedback arrives a tenth of a second or more late. Strong corrections using that late information can overshoot, correct back too late and swing, especially near the target.
cards.quote: a system that corrects strongly using late information tends to overshoot, correct back too late again, and swing.
cards.section: What goes wrong: movement without prediction

cards.front: Cerebellar signs are typically {{c1::ipsilateral}} to the lesion.
cards.back: Same side, because the output pathways cross twice.
cards.quote: Cerebellar signs are typically ipsilateral, and you can work out why.

cards.front: Trace the two crossings by which the left cerebellum controls the left arm through the corticospinal tract.
cards.back: Left dentate and interposed output leaves via the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses in the midbrain to the right ventrolateral thalamus, then right motor cortex. The corticospinal tract crosses back at the pyramidal decussation.
cards.quote: The corticospinal tract from the right cortex crosses back at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla and descends on the left.

cards.front: A patient has a lesion of the right dentate and interposed nuclei. Which arm is more likely to show dysmetria and intention tremor, and what is the common mistake?
cards.back: The right arm. Output crosses to the left thalamus and red nucleus, and the descending tracts cross back. Counting only one crossing gives the left arm.
cards.quote: Two crossings cancel: a left cerebellar lesion disturbs the left limbs.

cards.front: A small lesion destroys the right inferior olive. In the classical model, which half of the cerebellum loses its teaching signal, and which limbs would adapt poorly?
cards.back: The left cerebellum, because olivary climbing fibres cross. The left cerebellum acts on the left limbs through two crossings, so adaptation in the left limbs would suffer.
cards.why: Rests on: climbing fibres cross from olive to cerebellum, the climbing fibre is the teacher, and cerebellar output crosses twice.
cards.quote: The olivary climbing fibres also cross, so the right inferior olive teaches the left cerebellum.

cards.front: {{c1::Dysmetria}} is overshooting or undershooting a target, a limb sign of intermediate or lateral cerebellar damage.
cards.quote: dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting a target), dysdiadochokinesia (difficulty with fast alternating movements)

cards.front: How does cerebellar intention tremor differ from the tremor of Parkinson's disease?
cards.back: Intention tremor worsens as the limb nears its endpoint. Parkinsonian rest tremor is seen when the limb is still and relaxed, and starts with the basal ganglia.
cards.quote: Intention tremor is not the rest tremor of Parkinson's disease, which is seen when the limb is still and relaxed.

cards.front: A patient has an unsteady, wide-based gait but normal finger-to-nose testing in both arms and no nystagmus. Which cerebellar region is the most likely site of damage?
cards.back: The midline vermis (fastigial output) fits best on the rough map: it broadly serves posture, trunk and gait. But the zones overlap. Hemisphere damage can produce limb signs, and flocculonodular damage can produce gait ataxia and nystagmus; these findings are possible, not obligatory.
cards.why: The zones overlap, so the map is only a rough guide.
cards.quote: The zones overlap, so treat this as a rough guide.

cards.front: Is cerebellar damage purely motor?
cards.back: No. In patients with disease confined to the cerebellum, executive, visual-spatial and affective changes were described, most marked with posterior lobe and vermis lesions.
cards.quote: Schmahmann and Sherman (1998) described executive, visual-spatial and affective changes, most marked with lesions of the posterior lobe and vermis

cards.front: In one count of four adult male brains, about 69 billion of roughly 86 billion neurons sat in the cerebellum. What fraction is that, and which cell type makes up most cerebellar neurons?
cards.back: 69 / 86 = 0.80, about four in five of the brain's neurons. Most cerebellar neurons are granule cells.
cards.quote: about 69 billion of the roughly 86 billion (mean 86.1, standard deviation 8.1) neurons sat in the cerebellum
